title: Goals and advice for students: practice in small steps
summary: He sets goals for touring, film scoring and band pay, and advises students on simple practice goals, citing Wynton Marsalis's metronome practice.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: This has been really terrific. You know and I’m thinking you’re going to meet some students later on and I know that there are students here who want to be where you are. And I’m wondering if you — you’re obviously very goal oriented — what’s your goal for the next number of years and do you have other places that you want to get to?

Sure. I have a goal where I want to be much more, believe it or not, on tour with me and my own groups. I have goals where I’d like to write for a major motion picture or write for some type of film, to continue this. Goals to be a much better saxophonist. So you have goals to have earnings for your band. I want to be able to pay my musicians a certain amount of money. I want them to be able to earn a certain amount of money in a year with me. So then I’ll have the musicians consistent like I want them, if I’m able to

pay them, or keep them on enough of a basis where this money is coming along. But I do feel that you make that goal and you say well you know what, I’m going to learn a song a week for six months. So that’s something basic. So the first week “There’ll Never Be Another You.” Then the next week “I’ll Remember April.” Then the next week “’Round Midnight.” Then the next week – okay. And then once you memorize those songs, in six months, how many songs would you know. Or if you made a simple goal, I want to practice every day for one hour for six months, no matter what. Where would we be if we practiced every day for at least one hour, no matter what, for six months? You’re going to be a lot stronger than you are today. And within that, then you make little goals. Well what am I going to practice? You know Branford told me Wynton Marsalis, his brother, would get up in the morning and put on his metronome at 60. So [sings] dah dah de dah, dah dah de dah etc. That’s from Herbert Clarke Trumpet Studies. He practiced like that for six months. And one day he just woke up and [sings much faster] dah dah de dah etc. you know what I mean? So you’ve got to work towards — you’ve got to crawl, and you’ve got to walk, then you can run. You’ve got to make the baby steps. It’s just like anything that you’re doing, in terms of an educator or as a teacher, it started with a certain theme or thought process, now you have a skill set that you work from with respect to these interviews, how you go about it, the nature of it, the questions. It’s all a skill set. And so what the student has to realize is that it’s a skill set. And you have to figure, okay, what do I want to practice. And these are the things that I learned a little later, maybe I can share it with them, just so you don’t waste a lot of time. You can figure out what you want to practice, how you want to practice, the amount of time. Sometimes I’m learning now when you mind tells you I should stop, you keep going, that’s when you should stop. Just stop. If you’ve been practicing for three hours and your mind tells you to stop and you keep practicing, are you really still progressing or have you hit the wall? You’ve probably hit the wall. So the little things like that, but there’s so many little subtle things that we can do. You know again, I read all these kind of what most people call corny books, you know like one book I read one time said every time the phone rings, smile before you answer it. I tried it a couple of times and I said wow, the conversation always seems to be pleasant.
